danish.title: Fjortende bog (1812) — Kapitel 16
paragraphs: Efter den 28. oktober, da frosten satte ind, antog de franskes flugt en endnu mere tragisk karakter, med mænd der frøs ihjel eller blev stegt til døde ved lejrbålene, mens vogne med mennesker i pelsfrakker fortsat kørte forbi og fragtede det gods, kejseren, kongerne og hertugerne havde stjålet; men selve flugtens og den franske hærs opløsnings proces forløb i alt væsentligt som før.

Fra Moskva til Vjazma blev den franske hær på treoghalvfjerdstusind mand — garden ikke medregnet, da den intet andet foretog sig under hele krigen end at plyndre — reduceret til seksogtredive tusind, skønt højst fem tusind var faldet i kamp. Fra denne begyndelse kunne de følgende led i rækken bestemmes matematisk. Den franske hær smeltede bort og gik til grunde med samme hastighed fra Moskva til Vjazma, fra Vjazma til Smolensk, fra Smolensk til Berezina, og fra Berezina til Vilna — uafhængigt af kuldens større eller mindre intensitet, forfølgelsen, vejspærringerne eller nogen andre særlige omstændigheder. Hinsides Vjazma trængte den franske hær sig, i stedet for at marchere i tre kolonner, sammen til én masse og fortsatte således til enden. Berthier skrev til sin kejser (vi ved, hvor langt kommanderende officerer tillader sig at afvige fra sandheden i beskrivelsen af en hærs tilstand), og dette er hvad han sagde:

Jeg anser det for min pligt at indberette til Deres Majestæt tilstanden for de forskellige korps, jeg har haft lejlighed til at observere under forskellige etaper af de sidste to-tre dages march. De er næsten opløste. Knap en fjerdedel af soldaterne er tilbage ved deres regimenters faner, de øvrige går på egen hånd i forskellige retninger i håb om at finde føde og undslippe disciplinen. Generelt betragter de Smolensk som det sted, hvor de håber at komme sig. I de seneste dage er mange mænd set kaste deres patroner og våben fra sig. Under sådanne omstændigheder, uanset Deres Majestæts endelige planer, kræver tjenestens interesse, at hæren samles ved Smolensk og først og fremmest befris for unyttige elementer som afberedet kavaleri, overflødig bagage og artillerimateriel, der ikke længere står i forhold til de nuværende styrker. Soldaterne, som er udmattede af sult og træthed, har brug for disse forsyninger såvel som et par dages hvile. Mange er døde de seneste dage på vejen eller ved bivuakkerne. Denne tilstand forværres løbende og giver anledning til frygt for, at tropperne ikke længere kan kontrolleres i tilfælde af en træfning, medmindre der hurtigt gribes ind.
Da de tumlede ind i Smolensk, som forekom dem et forjættet land, slog franskmændene hinanden ihjel i jagten på mad, plyndrede deres egne depoter, og da alt var plyndret, flygtede de videre.

De drog alle videre uden at vide hvorhen eller hvorfor. Endnu mindre vidste det geni, Napoleon, det, for ingen udstedte nogen ordrer til ham. Men stadig bevarede han og hans omgivelser deres gamle vaner: skrev befalinger, breve, rapporter og dagsbefaling; kaldte hinanden sire, mon cousin, prince d'Eckmühl, roi de Naples og så videre. Men disse ordrer og rapporter eksisterede kun på papiret, intet af det blev udført, for det kunne ikke udføres, og skønt de titulerede hinanden Majestæter, Højheder eller Kousiner, følte de alle, at de var elendige stakler, der havde begået megen ondskab, som de nu måtte bøde for. Og skønt de lod, som om de bekymrede sig om hæren, tænkte enhver kun på sig selv og på, hvordan han hurtigst kunne komme væk og redde sig.

english.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: After October twenty-eighth, when the frosts set in, the French flight took on an even more tragic character. Men froze to death or burned themselves alive at campfires, while carriages carrying people dressed in furs continued to roll past, hauling away the property that had been stolen by the Emperor, kings, and dukes. But the essential nature of the flight and disintegration of the French army continued as before.

From Moscow to Vyazma, the French army of seventy-three thousand men—not counting the Guards, who did nothing during the entire war but loot—was reduced to thirty-six thousand, though no more than five thousand had fallen in battle. From this starting point, the terms of the progression could be calculated mathematically. The French army melted away and perished at the same rate from Moscow to Vyazma, from Vyazma to Smolensk, from Smolensk to the Berezina, and from the Berezina to Vilna—regardless of the cold's intensity, the pursuit, the blocking of their path, or any other particular conditions. Beyond Vyazma, the French army stopped moving in three columns and huddled together into one mass, continuing that way to the end. Berthier wrote to his Emperor (and we know how far commanding officers allow themselves to stray from the truth when describing their army's condition), and this is what he said:

I consider it my duty to report to Your Majesty on the condition of the various corps I have had the opportunity to observe during different stages of the last two or three days' march. They are nearly disbanded. Scarcely a quarter of the soldiers remain with the standards of their regiments; the others wander off in every direction hoping to find food and escape discipline. In general, they all look to Smolensk as the place where they hope to recover. During the last few days many soldiers have been seen throwing away their cartridges and their weapons. In such circumstances, whatever your ultimate plans may be, Your Majesty's interests require that the army be reassembled at Smolensk and, first of all, freed from noncombatants—dismounted cavalry, unnecessary baggage, and artillery equipment no longer proportionate to our present forces. The soldiers, worn out by hunger and fatigue, need these supplies as well as a few days' rest. Many have died recently on the road or at camp. This state of affairs is growing worse every day and raises the fear that, unless prompt measures are taken, the troops will be beyond control in the event of a battle.

After staggering into Smolensk—which had seemed to them a promised land—the French searched for food, killed one another, looted their own stores, and when everything had been plundered, fled farther.

They all went without knowing where or why they were going. Still less did that supposed genius, Napoleon, know it, for no one was issuing any orders to him. But he and those around him still clung to their old habits: writing commands, letters, reports, and orders of the day; calling one another "Sire," "Mon Cousin," "Prince of Eckmuhl," "King of Naples," and so on. But these orders and reports existed only on paper. Nothing in them was carried out, because nothing could be carried out. And though they addressed one another as Majesties, Highnesses, and Cousins, they all knew they were miserable wretches who had done great evil for which they now had to pay. And though they pretended to be concerned about the army, each was thinking only of himself and how to get away as quickly as possible.
